Finite-time blow-up in a quasilinear degenerate chemotaxis system with flux limitation

Yuka Chiyoda, Masaaki Mizukami** * Corresponding author†† † Partially supported by JSPS Research Fellowships for Young Scientists, No. 17J00101, Tomomi Yokota‡‡ ‡ Partially supported by Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (C), No. 16K05182.00 0 E-mail: g11914oboe@gmail.com, masaaki.mizukami.math@gmail.com, 00 0 yokota@rs.kagu.tus.ac.jp

Department of Mathematics, Tokyo University of Science

1-3, Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan

August 24, 2026

  • Abstract. This paper deals with the quasilinear degenerate chemotaxis system with flux limitation

    {ut=∇⋅(up∇uu2+|∇u|2)−χ∇⋅(uq∇v1+|∇v|2),x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−μ+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u^{p}\nabla u}{\sqrt{u^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u^{q}\nabla v}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla v|^{2}}}\right),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ 0=\Delta v-\mu+u,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{cases}

    where Ω:=BR​(0)⊂ℝn\Omega:=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) is a ball with some R>0R>0, and χ>0\chi>0, p,q≥1p,q\geq 1, μ:=1|Ω|​∫Ωu0\mu:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0} and u0u_{0} is an initial data of an unknown function uu. Bellomo–Winkler (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B;2017;4;31–67) established existence of an initial data such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time when p=q=1p=q=1. This paper gives existence of blow-up solutions under some condition for χ\chi and u0u_{0} when 1≤p≤q1\leq p\leq q.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the quasilinear degenerate chemotaxis system with flux limitation:

(1.1) {ut=∇⋅(up∇uu2+|∇u|2)−χ∇⋅(uq∇v1+|∇v|2),x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−μ+u,x∈Ω,t>0,(up∇uu2+|∇u|2−χ​uq∇v1+|∇v|2)⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ω,\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u^{p}\nabla u}{\sqrt{u^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u^{q}\nabla v}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla v|^{2}}}\right),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[5.69054pt] 0=\Delta v-\mu+u,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[5.69054pt] \left(\dfrac{u^{p}\nabla u}{\sqrt{u^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}}}-\chi\dfrac{u^{q}\nabla v}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla v|^{2}}}\right)\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\[14.22636pt] u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases}

where Ω=BR​(0)⊂ℝn​(n∈ℕ)\Omega=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}(n\in\mathbb{N}) is a ball with some R>0R>0, χ>0\chi>0, p,q≥1p,q\geq 1 and the initial data u0u_{0} is a function fulfilling that

(1.2) u0∈C3(Ω¯)is radially symmetric and positive inΩ¯with∂u0∂ν=0on∂Ω\displaystyle u_{0}\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega})\ \mbox{is radially symmetric and positive in}\ \overline{\Omega}\ \mbox{with}\ \frac{\partial u_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0\ \mbox{on}\ \partial\Omega

and where

(1.3) μ:=1|Ω|​∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x.\displaystyle\mu:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}{u_{0}(x)\,dx}.

The system (1.1) represents the situation such that a cellular slime moves towards higher concentrations of the chemical substance, and the unknown function u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) describes the density of cell and the unknown function v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) denotes the concentration of chemoattractant at x∈Ωx\in\Omega and t≥0t\geq 0. This model is development of the chemotaxis system

(1.4) ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),vt=Δv−v+u;\displaystyle u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\quad v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u;

thanks to effect of the flux limitation, the system (1.1) describes the case that cell diffusivity is suppressed; therefore the system (1.1) is innovative and important because it is considered a sensitive dynamics in aggregation phenomena.

Before we introduce previous works about the system (1.1), we will recall known results about the chemotaxis system (1.4):

The system (1.4) is proposed by Keller–Segel [10] and is called a Keller–Segel system. About the Keller–Segel system it was known that the size of the initial data in some Lebesgue norm determines behaviour of solutions; in the case that n=1n=1, Osaki–Yagi [16] obtained global existence and boundedness of classical solutions of (1.4); in the case that n=2n=2, it is shown that there is a critical value C>0C>0 (C=8​πC=8\pi in the radial setting and C=4​πC=4\pi in the other setting) such that, if ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)<C\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}<C then global solutions exist ([15]), and if m>Cm>C then there is an initial data satisfying that ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)=m\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}=m and the corresponding solution blows up in finite time ([6, 13]); in the case that n≥3n\geq 3, Horstmann–Winkler [7] asserted possibility of existence of unbounded solutions; Winkler [17] showed that for all m>0m>0 there exists an initial data such that ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)=m\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}=m and the corresponding solution blows up in finite time; also in the case that n=3n=3, Cao [3] established global existence and boundedness under the condition that ‖u0‖Ln2​(Ω)\|u_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{n}{2}}(\Omega)} and ‖∇v0‖Ln​(Ω)\|\nabla v_{0}\|_{L^{n}(\Omega)} are sufficiently small.

The Keller–Segel system (1.4) is now studied by many mathematicians intensively. Moreover, many variations of generalizations of the Keller–Segel system (1.4) are also sprightly studied. Here one of the important generalized problems is the degenerate chemotaxis system

ut=Δup−∇⋅(uq−1∇v),vt=Δv−v+u,u_{t}=\Delta u^{p}-\nabla\cdot(u^{q-1}\nabla v),\quad v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,

where p≥1p\geq 1, q≥2q\geq 2. This problem is one of the model which has a nonlinear diffusion suggested by Hillen–Painter [5], and it is shown that the relation between pp and qq determines behaviour of solutions; in the case q<p+2nq<p+\frac{2}{n}, global solutions are obtained when Ω\Omega is a bounded domain (see [8]). In the case q=p+2nq=p+\frac{2}{n}, the result is divided by the size of the initial data with some critical mass mc=mc​(n)m_{c}=m_{c}(n). When ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)=m<mc\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}=m<m_{c} and q=2q=2, under the Dirichlet–Neumann boundary condition, Mimura [12] showed that there are global solutions when Ω\Omega is a bounded domain. On the other hand, if m>mcm>m_{c}, then Laurençot–Mizoguchi [11] established that existence of an initial data such that ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)=m\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}=m and the corresponding solution blows up in finite time when q=2q=2, Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n} and n=3,4n=3,4. In the case q>p+2nq>p+\frac{2}{n}, it is known that there exists an initial data such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time (see [4]). Thus, it is clear that the relation between p,qp,q and nn strongly affects behaviour of solutions.

On the other hand, the system which describes the situation such that the movement of the species is suppressed, that is, the chemotaxis system with flux limitation

(1.5) {ut=∇⋅(Du​(u,v)​u∇uu2+|∇u|2)−∇⋅(S⁡(u,v)​u∇v1+|∇v|2)+H1​(u,v),vt=Dv​Δ​v+H2​(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(D_{u}(u,v)\dfrac{u\nabla u}{\sqrt{u^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)-\nabla\cdot\left(S(u,v)\dfrac{u\nabla v}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla v|^{2}}}\right)+H_{1}(u,v),&\\[14.22636pt] v_{t}=D_{v}\Delta v+H_{2}(u,v),\qquad x\in\Omega,\ t>0&\end{cases}

is proposed by Bellemo–Winkler [1], where DuD_{u} and DvD_{v} show properties of diffusion of the species and the chemoatractant, respectively, and SS represents the chemotactic interaction, and H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} are mechanisms of propagation, degeneration, and interaction. Since it has not been known whether there exist valid functions like an energy function and a Lyapunov function yet, the system (1.5) seems to be difficult. Therefore, Bellomo–Winkler [1, 2] have considered the following simplified system

(1.6) ut=∇⋅(u∇uu2+|∇u|2)−χ∇⋅(u∇v1+|∇v|2),0=Δv−μ+u.\displaystyle u_{t}=\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u\nabla u}{\sqrt{u^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}}}\right)-\chi\nabla\cdot\left(\dfrac{u\nabla v}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla v|^{2}}}\right),\quad 0=\Delta v-\mu+u.

In this system, Bellomo–Winkler [1] overcame the difficulty, and they showed global existence when χ<1\chi<1. On the other hand, if χ>1\chi>1 and

(1.7) {m>1χ2−1if​n=1,m>0​is arbitraryif​n≥2,\displaystyle\begin{cases}m>\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\chi^{2}-1}}&\mbox{if}\ n=1,\\[14.22636pt] m>0\ \mbox{is arbitrary}&\mbox{if}\ n\geq 2,\end{cases}

Bellomo–Winkler [2] found an initial data such that the corresponding solution of (1.6) blows up in finite time. However, the problem (1.5) has not been studied yet when DuD_{u} and SS are general; in view of the study of the Keller–Segel system, the case that Du​(u,v)=up−1D_{u}(u,v)=u^{p-1} and S⁡(u,v)=uq−1S(u,v)=u^{q-1} in (1.5), i.e., the system (1.1) seems to be one of important problems. Recently global existence of solutions to system (1.1) was shown when p>q+1−1np>q+1-\frac{1}{n} (see [14]). From the results in the degenerate chemotaxis system we can expect that some largeness condition for qq derives existence of blow-up solutions.

The purpose of this paper is to determine the condition for pp and qq such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time. Here we need to establish different methods because we cannot adopt the same argument as in [2] when p<qp<q holds.

Now main results read as follows.

Let Ω:=BR​(0)⊂ℝn\Omega:=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕ)(n\in\mathbb{N}) with R>0R>0 and suppose that 1≤p≤q1\leq p\leq q.

(i) If n=1n=1, then for all χ>1\chi>1 (χ>0𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸(\chi>0 when 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁q>p)q>p), there exists mc=mc​(χ,p,q,R)>0m_{c}=m_{c}(\chi,p,q,R)>0 with the following property: If

then there exists a nondecreasing function Mm∈C0​([0,R])M_{m}\in C^{0}([0,R]) satisfying supr∈(0,R)Mm​(r)|Br​(0)|<∞\sup_{r\in(0,R)}\frac{M_{m}(r)}{|B_{r}(0)|}<\infty,

Mm​(R)≤mM_{m}(R)\leq m, and that for all u0∈C3​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega}) with ∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x=m\int_{\Omega}{u_{0}(x)\,dx}=m and

for all r∈[0,R]r\in[0,R], there exists T∗∈(0,∞)T^{\ast}\in(0,\infty) such that a corresponding solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) blows up in finite time T∗T^{\ast} in the sense that

(1.10) lim supt↗T∗‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)=∞.\displaystyle\limsup_{t\nearrow T^{\ast}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=\infty.

(ii) If n≥2n\geq 2 and m>0m>0, then for all χ>0\chi>0 satisfying

(1.11) χ>(m​nωn​Rn)p−q,\displaystyle\chi>\left(\frac{mn}{\omega_{n}R^{n}}\right)^{p-q},

where ωn\omega_{n} defines the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional measure of the unit sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, there exists a nondecreasing function Mm∈C0​([0,R])M_{m}\in C^{0}([0,R]) satisfying supr∈(0,R)Mm​(r)|Br​(0)|<∞\sup_{r\in(0,R)}\frac{M_{m}(r)}{|B_{r}(0)|}<\infty, and Mm​(R)≤mM_{m}(R)\leq m, such that for all u0∈C3​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega}) with ∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x=m\int_{\Omega}{u_{0}(x)\,dx}=m and (1.9) for all r∈[0,R]r\in[0,R], there exists T∗∈(0,∞)T^{\ast}\in(0,\infty) such that the corresponding solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) blows up in finite time T∗T^{\ast} in the sense of (1.10).

Remark 1.1.

This theorem shows existence of blow-up solutions to (1.1) when q≥pq\geq p. On the other hand, in [14] global existence of solutions is shown when p>q+1−1np>q+1-\frac{1}{n}. However, except for the case n=1n=1, behaviour of solutions in the case q<p≤q+1−1nq<p\leq q+1-\frac{1}{n} is still an open problem (see Figure 1).

Remark 1.2.

If p=q=1p=q=1, then the condition for mm connects with that in [2]; indeed, the constant mc​(χ,p,q,R)m_{c}(\chi,p,q,R) in (1.8) is given by

mc=inf{m|∃λ∈(5−172,1];{1−(1−λ)23​λ−1}​m​χ1λ2+(1−λ)2λ2​(3​λ−1)+m2=(mωn⋅(1−λ)2λ⁡(λ+1)​R)p−q}m_{c}=\inf\left\{m\ \Bigg|\ \exists\,\lambda\in\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{17}}{2},1\right];\,\frac{\left\{1-\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{3\lambda-1}\right\}m\chi}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}+\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{\lambda^{2}(3\lambda-1)}+m^{2}}}=\left(\frac{m}{\omega_{n}}\cdot\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{\lambda(\lambda+1)R}\right)^{p-q}\right\}

(see (3.1) and (3.53)). Thus, in the case p=qp=q, since

mc​(χ,p,p,R)\displaystyle m_{c}(\chi,p,p,R) =inf{m|∃λ∈(5−172,1];{1−(1−λ)23​λ−1}​m​χ1λ2+(1−λ)2λ2​(3​λ−1)+m2=1}\displaystyle=\inf\left\{m\ \Bigg|\ \exists\,\lambda\in\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{17}}{2},1\right];\,\frac{\left\{1-\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{3\lambda-1}\right\}m\chi}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}+\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{\lambda^{2}(3\lambda-1)}+m^{2}}}=1\right\}
=inf{m|m​χ1+m2=1}=1χ2−1\displaystyle=\inf\left\{m\ \Bigg|\ \frac{m\chi}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}=1\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\chi^{2}-1}}

and moreover

(m​nωn​Rn)p−p=1,\left(\frac{mn}{\omega_{n}R^{n}}\right)^{p-p}=1,

the conditions (1.8) and (1.11) are reduced to (1.7). Thus Theorem 1.1 is a generalization of the previous work [2].

In view of Remark 1.2 we have the following corollary.

Let Ω:=BR​(0)⊂ℝn\Omega:=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕ)(n\in\mathbb{N}) with R>0R>0 and let p=q≥1p=q\geq 1, and suppose that χ>1\chi>1 and (1.7). Then there exists a nondecreasing function Mm∈C0​([0,R])M_{m}\in C^{0}([0,R]) fulfilling supr∈(0,R)Mm​(R)|Br​(0)|<∞\sup_{r\in(0,R)}\frac{M_{m}(R)}{|B_{r}(0)|}<\infty and Mm​(R)≤mM_{m}(R)\leq m, which is such that whenever u0u_{0} satisfies (1.2), as well as (1.9) for all r∈[0,R]r\in[0,R], the solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) blows up in finite time in the sense of (1.10).

Theorem 1.1 gives the following byproduct; since arguments similar to those in the proof of [2, Proposition 1.2] enable us to see this proposition, we only write the statement.

Proposition 1.3.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, R>0R>0, Ω:=BR​(0)⊂ℝn\Omega:=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and χ>1\chi>1.

(i) Let m>0m>0 satisfy (1.8). Then there exists a radially symmetric positive um∈C∞​(Ω¯)u_{m}\in C^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}) which is such that

∂um∂ν=0​on​∂Ωand​∫Ωum=m,\frac{\partial u_{m}}{\partial\nu}=0\ \mbox{on}\ \partial\Omega\quad\mbox{and}\ \int_{\Omega}{u_{m}}=m,

and for which it is possible to choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 with the property that whenever u0u_{0} satisfies (1.2) as well as

‖u0−um‖L∞​(Ω)≤ε,\|u_{0}-u_{m}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\varepsilon,

the corresponding solution of (1.1) blows up in finite time.

(ii) Given any u0u_{0} fulfilling (1.2), one can find functions u0​ku_{0k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, which satisfy (1.2) and

u0​k→u0in​Lp​(Ω)as​k→∞u_{0k}\to u_{0}\quad\mbox{in}\ L^{p}(\Omega)\quad\mbox{as}\ k\to\infty

for all p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), and which are such that for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} the solution of (1.1) emanating from u0​ku_{0k} blows up in finite time.

The proof of the main result is based on that of [2, Theorem1.1]. Thus in the same way, we introduce s:=rns:=r^{n} for r∈[0,R]r\in[0,R] and the mass accumulation function w=w⁡(s,t)w=w(s,t) defined as

w⁡(s,t):=∫0s1nrn−1​u​(r,t)​𝑑r,w(s,t):=\int_{0}^{s^{\frac{1}{n}}}{r^{n-1}u(r,t)\,dr},

and then, a combination of the fact u⁡(r∗,t)≥w⁡(s∗,t)s∗u(r_{\ast},t)\geq\frac{w(s_{\ast},t)}{s_{\ast}} given by using u≥wsu\geq w_{s} and the mean value theorem and that ww is the solution of a scalar parabolic equation yields that the core of the proof is to find a suitable subsolution w¯\underline{w} such that for some T>0T>0 and some s∗∈(0,Rn)s_{\ast}\in(0,R^{n}),

w¯​(s∗,t)s∗→∞​as​t↗T.\displaystyle\frac{\underline{w}(s_{\ast},t)}{s_{\ast}}\to\infty\ \mbox{as}\ t\nearrow T.

In the previous study [2], the interval (0,Rn)(0,R^{n}) is divided three parts, and in very inner region thanks to construction of the subsolution w¯\underline{w} using the structure of a quadratic function, we obtain a suitable estimate. However, in this paper we cannot establish it from the same argument when p<qp<q. Therefore, adopting a new subsolution w¯\underline{w} consisted by an exponential function, we can prove existence of an initial data such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time. In this proof, the key idea is to employ a new viewpoint in the proof of some suitable estimate; by establishing a new estimate where the effect of the aggregation come from chemotactic interaction works adequately (see Lemma 3.5), we can attain a useful estimate.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall local existence in (1.1) and we consider the mass accumulation function and a scalar parabolic equation. In order to use the comparison argument as in [2, Lemma 5.1] we construct subsolutions and confirm properties in Section 3. Finally, we prove existence of blow-up solutions in Section 4.

2 Local existence and a parabolic problem satisfied by the mass accumulation

In this section we provide a local existence result and a mass accumulation satisfies some parabolic problem. First, we recall a local existence result; the following result was shown in [14, Theorem 1.1].

Lemma 2.1.

Suppose that u0u_{0} complies with (1.2). Then there exist Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\rm max}\in(0,\infty] and a pair (u,v)(u,v) of positive radially symmetric functions u∈C2,1​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))u\in C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\rm max})) and v∈C2,0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))v\in C^{2,0}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\rm max})) which solve (1.1) classically in Ω×(0,Tmax)\Omega\times(0,T_{\rm max}), and which are such that

(2.1) ifTmax<∞,thenlim supt↗Tmax‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)=∞.\displaystyle\mbox{if}\quad T_{\rm max}<\infty,\quad\mbox{then}\quad\limsup_{t\nearrow T_{\rm max}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=\infty.

In the following let Ω:=BR​(0)⊂ℝn\Omega:=B_{R}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) with some R>0R>0 and let u0u_{0} satisfy (1.2), and denote by (u,v)=(u⁡(r,t),v⁡(r,t))(u,v)=(u(r,t),v(r,t)) the radially symmetric local solution of (1.1) and by TmaxT_{\rm max} its maximal existence time obtained in Lemma 2.1. Moreover, we introduce the mass accumulation function ww and the parabolic operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that

(2.2) w⁡(s,t):=∫0s1nrn−1​u​(r,t)​𝑑r\displaystyle w(s,t):=\int_{0}^{s^{\frac{1}{n}}}{r^{n-1}u(r,t)\,dr}

for s∈[0,Rn]s\in[0,R^{n}] and t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T), and

(2.3) (𝒫​w~)​(s,t):=w~t−np+1⋅s2−2n​w~sp​w~s​sw~s2+n2​s2−2n​w~s​s2−nq​χ⋅(w~−μn​s)​w~sq1+s2n−2​(w~−μn​s)2.\displaystyle(\mathcal{P}\widetilde{w})(s,t):=\widetilde{w}_{t}-n^{p+1}\cdot\frac{s^{2-\frac{2}{n}}\widetilde{w}_{s}^{p}\widetilde{w}_{ss}}{\sqrt{\widetilde{w}_{s}^{2}+n^{2}s^{2-\frac{2}{n}}\widetilde{w}_{ss}^{2}}}-n^{q}\chi\cdot\frac{(\widetilde{w}-\frac{\mu}{n}s)\widetilde{w}_{s}^{q}}{\sqrt{1+s^{\frac{2}{n}-2}(\widetilde{w}-\frac{\mu}{n}s)^{2}}}.

If w~∈C1​((0,Rn)×(0,T))\widetilde{w}\in C^{1}((0,R^{n})\times(0,T)) is such that w~s>0\widetilde{w}_{s}>0 and w~​(⋅,t)∈W2,∞​(0,Rn)\widetilde{w}(\cdot,t)\in W^{2,\infty}(0,R^{n}) for all t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T), then the expression 𝒫​w~\mathcal{P}\widetilde{w} is well-defined. Now we show that the function ww defined as (2.2) fulfills these corresponding condition. Thus, the following lemma yields that the function ww satisfies some parabolic problem (see [2, Lemma 2.1]).

Lemma 2.2.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, χ>0\chi>0. Then for T>0T>0 and some nonnegative radially symmetric u0∈C0​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}), whenever (u,v)(u,v) is a positive radially symmetric classical solution of (1.1) in Ω×[0,T)\Omega\times[0,T), the function ww defined as (2.2) satisfies

(2.4) {(𝒫​w)​(s,t)=0,s∈(0,Rn),t∈(0,T),w(0,t)=0,w(Rn,t)=mωn,t∈(0,T),w⁡(s,0)=∫0s1nrn−1​u0​(r)​dr,s∈[0,Rn],\displaystyle\begin{cases}(\mathcal{P}w)(s,t)=0,&s\in(0,R^{n}),\ t\in(0,T),\\ w(0,t)=0,\quad w(R^{n},t)=\dfrac{m}{\omega_{n}},&t\in(0,T),\\ w(s,0)=\int_{0}^{s^{\frac{1}{n}}}{r^{n-1}u_{0}(r)\,dr},&s\in[0,R^{n}],\end{cases}

An argument similar to that in the proof of [2, Lemma 2.1] implies the conclusion of this lemma. ∎

3 Construction of subsolutions for (2.4)

In this section we construct a subsolution w¯\underline{w} of (2.4). Then, using a suitable comparison principle (see [2, Lemma 5.1]) to obtain w≥w¯w\geq\underline{w} in [0,Rn]×[0,T)[0,R^{n}]\times[0,T), we derive that u⁡(r,t)u(r,t) blows up in finite time T>0T>0 (fixed later). In Section 3.1 we prepare a family of functions, and define w¯\underline{w}. In Sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 we divide [0,Rn][0,R^{n}] into three parts and show properties of a subsolution w¯\underline{w} in respective regions.
